title: The Acacia and the Herdsman’s Promise
summary: A young herder promises the acacia a share of every milking if the tree will shade his cattle through the long dry season.
moral: A promise given to a tree is still a promise.
attribution: A traditional Maasai tale, retold for Ubuntu Tales.

cover.alt: A flat-topped acacia against a wide sun, with cattle silhouettes crossing the savanna

sentences.text: When the long dry season came, the grass turned the colour of old rope and the waterholes shrank from one valley to the next.
A young herder named Lelesiit drove his cattle far from home, searching for a place where they could rest.
At noon, he found one tree with a wide flat crown, an acacia that spread its branches like a roof.
He stopped beneath it and let the cattle shade themselves.
The tree stood at the edge of a dry and ancient watercourse, and its shadow was the only cool thing for a day’s walk in any direction.
The herder was grateful, and he was also afraid, because a man alone with thirsty cattle gives promises easily.
He poured a little milk at the foot of the tree and said, “If you keep my herd alive until the rains, a share of every milking will be yours, and my children will know your name.”
The acacia did nothing that a tree can do.
The herd rested and did not lose flesh, and on the third night the clouds built up and the rain came down out of the dark.
The cattle drank, and the grass came up green through the dust.
When the herder returned home, he remembered his promise.
Some of the other men laughed at him.
“It is only a tree,” they said.
But Lelesiit poured a little of every milking at the root of the acacia near his home, and he told his children to do the same.
And the acacia has never lost its thorns, and has never needed anyone’s thanks, but it still opens its branches wide for the herds.
The old people say this is why a promise must be kept even when the one you promised it to can never ask you to keep it.
